messages.content: Contemplate on few lines of “Part four” (page 153) of this novel, “Majid: Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village. When Majeed came out of the house carrying Jamila, wrapped in a thin... quilt, a bewilderedRahima at his heels, the brilliant moonlight at first blinded him.” Even if Majeed was mostly depicted as a cunning and apathetic person throughout the narrative, do you find the same character traits in the mentioned lines? Was he trying to save Rahima and Jamila out of good-will (deontology) or his action was well-calculated (teleology)?Explain it. Include at least 10 single-word palindromes, each at least 5 characters long.

message.content:
Assuming “Majid” and “Majeed” refer to the same character, these lines do not simply confirm him as cunning and apathetic. On the surface, he is active, urgent, and protective: he wakes Rahima, carries Jamila wrapped in a thin quilt, and takes both of them toward the village. That is not the behavior of someone who is merely indifferent. There is responsibility in his movement, and the image of Rahima following “at his heels” suggests that he is directing their survival.

However, the same lines do not fully erase his earlier traits. His speech is controlled and strategic: “I am going to take both of you to the village.” This sounds less like a spontaneous burst of compassion and more like a man calculating the next step. He is not only rescuing them; he is choosing a destination, managing a risky moment, and keeping control. In that sense, his cunning may still be present, even if his apathy is temporarily suspended by the immediate danger or necessity.

If we judge his action through ethics, a deontological reading would say that Majeed is saving Rahima and Jamila because it is intrinsically right: their lives matter, and he is doing his duty regardless of the consequences. The passage contains hints of this—especially his physical effort to carry Jamila and his decision to bring both of them—so a purely selfish explanation would be too simple. Yet the lines do not give us enough to prove pure good-will.

A teleological reading fits better. His action is directed toward a future outcome: the village. That destination may mean safety, concealment, escape, or even self-preservation. The “brilliant moonlight” that “at first blinded him” also reinforces the sense of risk and calculation; he is moving through a visible, dangerous space, and his decision is tied to what will happen next. So his rescue can be read as well-calculated rather than purely moral, perhaps mixed with genuine concern but not wholly selfless.

Palindromic anchors, all single words of at least five letters: level, radar, civic, rotor, refer, madam, tenet, peeper, reviver, deified, racecar, redder.
